usage: Sino-Korean reading of 0; used in numbers, scores, temperatures
examples: The score is zero to zero.
There's zero won in my account.
nuance: 영 is the Sino-Korean word for zero, used in math, scores, temperatures, and decimals. For zeros inside phone numbers, Koreans usually say 공 instead. Both mean 'zero,' but they are not interchangeable in every context.
mistakes: Saying 영 for the 0 in a phone number — use 공 there
Confusing 영 (zero) with the native counting that has no word for zero

usage: the 0 read aloud in phone numbers and room numbers
공 reads the 0 inside the number
nuance: 공 is how Koreans say the digit zero when reading phone numbers, room numbers, and similar strings of digits. In math or temperature you say 영 instead. Beginners must know both because phone numbers come up constantly.
mistakes: Using 영 for the 0 in 010 — natives say 공일공
Reading 공 as the native number 'zero' — there is no native zero

usage: but native 스무 명 is more common in speech
examples: The bus comes in twenty minutes.
nuance: 이십 is the Sino-Korean twenty, used for minutes, dates, money, and phone numbers. For counting ages, hours, or people, the native form 스물/스무 is often used instead. Knowing which system to use is one of the first big steps for a Korean beginner.
mistakes: Using 이십 for the hour — clocks use native 두 시, not 이 시
Mixing it up with native 스물 when both could appear

nuance: 삼십 is the Sino-Korean thirty, essential for telling time since '30 minutes' (half past) comes up constantly. It also reads dates, seconds, and prices. Pair it with native hours: '7:30' is 일곱 시 삼십 분.
mistakes: Saying 삼십 시 for an hour — hours are native (일곱 시)
Dropping 분 and just saying the number when telling time

nuance: 사십 is the Sino-Korean forty, used for minutes, prices, and durations. As with all Sino numbers, you stack the ones digit after it: 사십오 is 45. It does not replace the native forty (마흔) used for age.
mistakes: Using 사십 for someone's age — age uses native 마흔
Pronouncing 사 too short so it sounds like another number

examples: Please give me fifty more won.
nuance: 오십 is the Sino-Korean fifty, common for minutes, money, and percentages (sales). Like other tens, it combines with ones: 오십삼 is 53. Use it for prices and time, not for age, where native 쉰 is used.
mistakes: Saying 오십 시 for an hour — hours are native
Confusing the sound of 오십 with 오 (five) alone

examples: It took sixty minutes to get here.
nuance: 육십 is the Sino-Korean sixty, used for seconds, minutes, durations, and formal ages with 세. Note that 육 is pronounced softly and links to 십. For casual age you would hear native 예순 instead of 육십.
mistakes: Using native 예순 with 세 — 세 pairs with Sino 육십
Forgetting that 육 changes sound when linked (육십)

examples: I got seventy points on the test.
nuance: 칠십 is the Sino-Korean seventy, used for scores, distances, prices, and formal ages. It combines with ones like every Sino ten: 칠십이 is 72. The casual age word is native 일흔.
mistakes: Saying 칠십 for hours on a clock — that never happens
Mixing native 일흔 with formal counters that need Sino 칠십

examples: The battery is at eighty percent.
The test score is eighty points.
Go just eighty meters from here.
nuance: 팔십 is the Sino-Korean eighty, common for scores, percentages, and distances. Like other tens it stacks ones after it: 팔십육 is 86. For casual age, Koreans use the native 여든.
mistakes: Using 팔십 to count people casually — native counters differ
Confusing the sound 팔 with another digit when spoken fast

examples: My phone is ninety percent charged.
nuance: 구십 is the Sino-Korean ninety, the last of the tens before 백 (hundred). It is used for scores, percentages, and money, and stacks ones after it (구십삼 = 93). The casual age word is native 아흔.
mistakes: Saying 십구 (19) when you mean 구십 (90) — order matters
Using 구십 with hours — clocks use native numbers

examples: This laptop is one million won.
My monthly salary is two million won.
This city has a million people.
nuance: 백만 means one million and is built from 백 (hundred) times 만 (ten-thousand), since Korean groups large numbers by 만. Prices, salaries, and rent in Korea are often in the millions of won, so beginners meet 백만 quickly. Remember the grouping is by 4 digits (만), not 3.
mistakes: Counting in thousands like English — Korean groups by 만 (10,000)
Saying 천천 instead of 만 for ten-thousand

usage: the next big unit after 만
examples: I won 100 million won in the lottery.
This car is over 100 million won.
nuance: 억 is the unit for a hundred million and is essential in Korea because apartment and house prices are usually quoted in 억. It comes right after 만 in the big-number grouping (만 → 억). Even beginners hear it constantly in real-estate and salary talk.
mistakes: Confusing 억 (100 million) with 만 (10,000)
Trying to map 억 onto English 'million' — it is a hundred million

usage: counter for assigned numbers; with Sino numbers
asking for a bus, room, or question number
nuance: 번 is the counter for assigned numbers — bus numbers, exit numbers, exam questions, and order — and it always pairs with Sino-Korean numbers (삼 번, not 세 번 here). Note 번 also means 'times' for counting occurrences, but then it takes native numbers (세 번 = three times). Context tells the two apart.
mistakes: Using native numbers for bus/exit numbers — say 삼 번, not 세 번
Mixing 번(order, Sino) with 번(times, native)

usage: counter for building floors; with Sino numbers
asking in an elevator or store
examples: The restroom is on the second floor.
What floor are you going to?
The restaurant is on basement level 1.
nuance: 층 means a floor of a building and always takes Sino-Korean numbers: 일 층, 이 층, 삼 층. It is one of the most useful counters for daily life — shopping malls, apartments, and offices all use it. The basement is 지하 + Sino number (지하 일 층 = B1).
mistakes: Using native numbers with 층 — say 삼 층, not 세 층
Forgetting 지하 for basement floors (지하 일 층)
